herodion-asyncritus-phlegon.life: Herodion, Asyncritus and Phlegon were counted among the Seventy Apostles sent out by Christ, and Paul names them in his Epistle to the Romans. According to the account read, Herodion was a kinsman and travelling companion of Paul and served as bishop of Patara, Asyncritus as bishop in Hyrcania, and Phlegon in Marathon in Thrace. They are said to have suffered greatly and to have won a martyr's crown.

eupsychios-caesarea.life: Eupsychios, born in Caesarea in Cappadocia, was a newly married Christian when, under Julian the Apostate, he tore down the city's temple of Fortuna. After giving his goods to the poor, he endured the rack and iron claws and was beheaded. The Christians of Caesarea later built a church over his grave, where healings were reported.

terence-pompeius-companions.life: Terence and forty companions were Christians of Africa who refused the sacrifice ordered by Decius, and the governor Fortunianus had thirty-six of them beheaded. Terence, Pompeius, Africanus and Maximus were kept in prison, where tradition holds they were fed by an angel and unharmed by snakes. They were afterward beheaded, and Christians buried their bodies outside the city.

antipas-pergamon.life: Antipas, a disciple of John the Theologian, was bishop of Pergamum. He is named as a faithful martyr in the Book of Revelation. After he turned many from pagan sacrifice, the priests are said to have put him inside a heated bronze bull at the temple of Artemis. Christians buried him, and he is invoked for toothache.
antipas-pergamon.flags: App notes give ca. 92 AD; OCA dates his death to the reign of Nero (ca. 68). Sources differ, so no precise date is given in the life.

basil-bishop-parium.life: Basil, bishop of Parium, lived in the eighth century and was chosen bishop by the people who revered him as a true shepherd. When the iconoclast emperor Constantine V convened the Council of 754, he refused to sign its decree against icons and kept the heretics out of his diocese. He endured persecution, hunger and hardship, and stayed faithful to the Orthodox Church until his death.
basil-bishop-parium.flags: App lists him as 'Hieromartyr' with '+3rd c.'; OCA calls him Basil the Confessor, Bishop of Parium, 8th century, an iconoclast-era confessor who died in peace, not a martyr. Orthocal also lists 'St Basil the Confessor'. Type/title/century in app likely need correcting.

martin-confessor-pope.life: Martin, a native of Tuscany, became Pope of Rome in 649 and convened the Lateran Council, which condemned Monothelitism. The emperor Constans II had him seized, held on Naxos, and tried in Constantinople on false charges. Sentenced to death, he was instead exiled to Cherson in the Crimea, where he died in 655 from illness and hardship. He is honored as a confessor.

aristarchus-pudens-trophimus.life: Aristarchus, Pudens and Trophimus were counted among the Seventy Apostles and appear in Acts and in Paul's epistles. Aristarchus, Paul's travelling companion, became bishop of Apamea in Syria. Pudens, a Roman senator, received Peter and Paul in his house, and is said to have been martyred under Nero. Trophimus, from Edessa, was Paul's disciple and companion.

symeon-bishop-persia.life: Symeon, bishop in Persia, was brought in chains before the emperor Sapor II after a tax on Christians was imposed, and was accused of siding with Rome. He refused to worship the sun. The priests Habdelai and Ananias and many others were beheaded in front of him, and Symeon was executed last. OCA gives the date as April 13, 344.
symeon-bishop-persia.flags: App notes give +341 and place the saint at Seleucia-Ctesiphon; OCA gives 344 and does not name the see. Sources differ on the year; the life gives OCA's date.

john-disciple-gregory-theologian.life: John, born at the end of the eighth century, became a disciple of Gregory of Decapolis and was tonsured by him at a monastery in Thessalonica. When the iconoclast persecution was renewed under Leo the Armenian, he went with Gregory and Joseph the Hymnographer to Constantinople, where they defended the veneration of icons. He died soon after Gregory, and Joseph moved their relics.
john-disciple-gregory-theologian.flags: App name says disciple of 'St. Gregory the Theologian'; OCA and Orthocal name him disciple of Gregory of Decapolis (Nov 20). Same commemoration (April 18), but the name in the app appears wrong.

john-of-old-lavra.life: John lived in the eighth century in the Lavra of Saint Chariton, called the Old or Ancient Lavra, near Bethlehem and the Dead Sea. In his youth he left the world, venerated the holy places of Jerusalem and settled at the Lavra. He lived there in fasting, vigil and prayer, was ordained to the priesthood, and became known for his ascetic life.

anastasia-rome-martyr.flags: OCA April 20 lists Theodore Trichinas, Athanasios of Meteora, Apostle Zaccheus, and others; no Anastasia of Rome appears there, and Orthocal 4/20 names only Theodore Trichinas, Athanasios of Meteora and Zaccheus. OCA places 'Martyrs Basilissa and Anastasia of Rome, disciples of the Apostles' on April 15 (1st c., under Nero). Date mismatch or different identity; no life written.

januarius-bishop-beneventum.life: Januarius, bishop of Benevento, was arrested in Diocletian's persecution around 305. Tradition holds he came out of a furnace unharmed and that wild beasts in the arena would not touch him and his companions, the deacons Proculus, Sossius and Faustus, the reader Desiderius, and the laymen Eutychius and Acutius. The governor Menignus lost his sight and regained it through the bishop's prayer. They were afterward beheaded.

elizabeth-wonderworker.life: Elizabeth, from Constantinople, was dedicated to God from birth and was chosen abbess of the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian. She wore a hairshirt, kept strict fasts and received the gift of healing. Healings were reported at her tomb, and her relics were buried in the church of Saint George, where they remained incorrupt. OCA says her dates are uncertain.

basil-bishop-amasea.life: Basil became bishop of Amaseia in the fourth century and attended the councils of Ankyra and Neocaesarea in 314-315. Under Licinius he sheltered the maiden Glaphyra, who had fled the emperor, and he was summoned to Nikomedia. There he refused to sacrifice and was beheaded around 322. His body was recovered from the sea and buried in Amaseia.
basil-bishop-amasea.flags: OCA gives the account in detail; Wikipedia notes the Acts of his martyrdom are considered legendary. Life keeps to the core facts (bishop under Licinius, martyred c. 322).

simeon-bishop-jerusalem.life: Simeon, a kinsman of the Lord and son of Cleopas, succeeded James as bishop of Jerusalem. He is counted among the Seventy Apostles. He was denounced as a descendant of David and a Christian, and under the emperor Trajan was tortured and crucified. OCA gives the year as 107, when he was said to be over a hundred and twenty years old.

jason-sosipater.life: Jason of Tarsus and Sosipater of Patras were disciples of Paul, who calls them his kinsmen in Romans. Made bishops of Tarsus and Iconium, they traveled west and reached Corfu in the year 63, where they built a church, baptized many and were imprisoned. They won the governor's conversion and built more churches. They are said to have lived there into old age.

memnou-memnon-wonder-worker.life: Memnon lived from his youth in the Egyptian desert and became abbot of one of its monasteries, guiding the brothers with care. He was given the gift of clairvoyance. At his prayer a spring is said to have flowed in the wilderness and a plague of locusts perished. After his death, invoking his name was said to have saved shipwrecked sailors and to have driven off locusts.
memnou-memnon-wonder-worker.flags: App calls him 'Holy Martyr Memnon the Wonder-Worker (+3rd c.)'; OCA lists 'Venerable Memnon the Wonderworker', an Egyptian desert abbot, with no martyrdom and no century given. Orthocal for April 29 does not list him. Type and period in app need checking.

prophet-jeremiah.life: Jeremiah, son of the priest Helkiah of Anathoth, was called to prophesy as a youth in about the seventh to sixth century B.C. He denounced Judah's idolatry and foretold the Babylonian conquest, and was thrown into a pit and imprisoned. After Jerusalem fell he mourned its ruin and was taken to Egypt. Tradition holds he was killed there by his own people.

timothy-maura-martyrs.life: Timothy, a reader in the Thebaid, and his wife Maura, married only twenty days, were arrested in Diocletian's persecution after he refused to surrender the church's books. He was blinded and tortured, and Maura was tormented and urged to deny Christ. Both stood firm, and the governor Arian had them crucified facing each other. They died on the tenth day, in 286.

pelagia-tarsus.life: Pelagia of Tarsus, daughter of pagan parents, came to faith and chose a life of virginity. She was baptized by Bishop Linus and refused to marry the emperor's adopted heir, and later Diocletian himself. Diocletian ordered her put into a heated bronze bull. Her bones are said to have been guarded by lions until Bishop Linus buried them.

hiob-righteous.life: Job, the righteous man of the land of Ausis, was blessed with wealth and children, then lost all and was struck with sores. He bore this with thanks to God. OCA says that God later restored his prosperity twofold and that he lived long afterward. The Church reads the Book of Job in Holy Week, seeing a parallel with Christ's suffering.

appearance-cross-jerusalem.life: This feast recalls the appearance of a luminous Cross in the sky over Jerusalem on the morning of May 7, 351, in the reign of Constantius. Reaching from Golgotha to the Mount of Olives, it was described by Patriarch Cyril of Jerusalem in a letter to the emperor, and Sozomen reports that it led many to the faith.

isaiah-prophet.life: Isaiah, of royal lineage, prophesied for about sixty years under the kings of Judah, beginning with a vision of the Lord surrounded by seraphim. His book foretells the captivity and return of the Jews and the coming of Christ, so he is called the Old Testament evangelist. By tradition he drew forth the spring of Siloam, and King Manasseh had him sawn in two.

epiphanius-cyprus.life: Epiphanius, born in Phoenicia, became a monk under Hilarion the Great and was consecrated bishop of Salamis in Cyprus in 367. He was known for his zeal for the faith, his almsgiving and his writings against heresies, notably the Panarion. He left a council against John Chrysostom, and died at sea in 403. The Seventh Ecumenical Council named him a Father of the Church.

germanus-constantinople.life: Germanus, born in Constantinople in the seventh century, became bishop of Cyzicus and then Patriarch of Constantinople. He opposed the iconoclasm of Leo III and was forced to resign after about fourteen years. He spent his last years in a monastery and died in about 740. He wrote on the liturgy and on icons, and the Seventh Council named him among the saints.
germanus-constantinople.flags: Orthocal's May 12 list names only Epiphanius; OCA's May 12 page includes Germanus the Patriarch, so the commemoration is confirmed there.

glyceria-martyr.life: Glyceria, from a prominent family, became a Christian in Trajanopolis in Thrace. When the prefect Sabinus ordered a sacrifice to Zeus, she is said to have entered the temple and prayed, and the idol fell and broke. She was imprisoned, tortured and miraculously preserved, and was killed by a lioness at Heraclea. OCA's account places her under the emperor Antoninus.
glyceria-martyr.flags: App notes say +177 under Marcus Aurelius; OCA says second century under Antoninus (138-161). Sources differ; life omits the emperor's name and exact date.

isidore-chios.life: Isidore, an Egyptian from Alexandria, was an officer in the Roman fleet during the reign of Decius when it anchored off Chios. A centurion denounced him as a Christian. He refused to sacrifice, was tortured, and was beheaded. The Christian Myrope buried his body and later died in prison. A chapel was built over their graves.

theodotus-ancyra.flags: App date is 05-16. OCA May 16 and Orthocal 5/16 do not name Theodotus; both list Martyr Theodotus of Ancyra (innkeeper, with the seven virgins, under Decius/Diocletian) on May 18. Date mismatch; no life written.

andronicus-junia-apostles.life: Andronicus and Junia, kinsmen and fellow prisoners of Paul, are named in Romans 16:7 as notable among the apostles. Andronicus became bishop of Pannonia, and the two preached in many lands, converting pagans and building churches. The church's service says they were martyred. Their relics were found near Constantinople in the fifth century, where a church was built over the place.

peter-caesarea-cappadocia.flags: OCA May 18 names Martyr Theodotus of Ancyra and the Martyrs Peter, Dionysius, Andrew, Paul, Christina (Lampsacus, under Decius); Orthocal 5/18 similar. No 'Venerable Peter of Caesarea in Cappadocia' appears for May 18 (nor on May 16/17 OCA pages checked). Unidentified; no life written.

patrick-bishop-prusa.life: Patrick, bishop of Prusa in Bithynia, preached Christ openly and denounced pagan error. He and the priests Acacius, Menander and Polyainus were arrested and brought to the prefect Julius, who had Patrick thrown into a hot spring, where he was unharmed. All four were beheaded, around the year 100.
